entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12378"/><div sID="gen22657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12378"/><hi type="bold">10. my desire ... chastise--</hi>expressing God's strong inclination to vindicate His justice against sin, as being the infinitely holy God (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.63">De 28:63</reference>).<div eID="gen22657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people--</hi>Foreign invaders "shall be gathered against them."<div eID="gen22658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when they shall bind themselves in their two furrows--</hi>image from two oxen ploughing together side by side, in two contiguous furrows: so the Israelites shall join themselves, to unite their powers against all dangers, but it will not save them from My destroying them [Calvin]. Their "two furrows" may refer to their two places of setting up the calves, their ground of confidence, Dan and Beth-el; or, the two divisions of the nation, Israel and Judah, "in their two furrows," that is, in their respective two places of habitation; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference>, which specifies the two, favors this view. Henderson prefers the Keri (Hebrew Margin) "for their two iniquities"; and translates, "when they are bound" in captivity. English Version is best, as the image is carried out in <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference>; only it is perhaps better to translate, "the people (the invaders) binding them," that is, making them captives; and so <reference osisRef="Hos.10.11">Ho 10:11</reference> alludes to the yoke being put on the neck of Ephraim and Judah. <div eID="gen22659" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12379"/><div sID="gen22660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12379"/><hi type="bold">11. taught--</hi>that is, accustomed.<div eID="gen22660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loveth to tread out ... corn--</hi>a far easier and more self-indulgent work than ploughing. In treading corn, cattle were not bound together under a yoke, but either trod it singly with their feet, or drew a threshing sledge over it (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Is 28:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">28</reference>): they were free to eat some of the corn from time to time, as the law required they should be unmuzzled (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">De 25:4</reference>), so that they grew fat in this work. An image of Israel's freedom, prosperity, and self-indulgence heretofore. But now God will put the Assyrian yoke upon her, instead of freedom, putting her to servile work.<div eID="gen22661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I passed over upon--</hi>I put the yoke upon.<div eID="gen22662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make ... to ride--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.22">Job 30:22</reference>; that is, hurry Ephraim away to a distant region [Calvin]. Lyra translates, "I will make (the Assyrian) to ride upon Ephraim." Maurer, "I will make Ephraim to carry," namely, a charioteer.<div eID="gen22663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his clods--</hi>"the clods before him." <div eID="gen22664" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 11. taught-- that is, accustomed. loveth to tread out ... corn-- a far easier and more self-indulgent work than ploughing. In treading corn, cattle were not bound together under a yoke, but either trod it singly with their feet, or drew a threshing sledge over it ( Is 28:27 , 28 ): they were free to eat some of the corn from time to time, as the law required they should be unmuzzled ( De 25:4 ), so that they grew fat in this work. An image of Israel's freedom, prosperity, and self-indulgence heretofore. But now God will put the Assyrian yoke upon her, instead of freedom, putting her to servile work. I passed over upon-- I put the yoke upon. make ... to ride-- as in Job 30:22 ; that is, hurry Ephraim away to a distant region [Calvin]. entries.reader_content_plain: 11. taught-- that is, accustomed. loveth to tread out ... corn-- a far easier and more self-indulgent work than ploughing. In treading corn, cattle were not bound together under a yoke, but either trod it singly with their feet, or drew a threshing sledge over it ( Is 28:27 , 28 ): they were free to eat some of the corn from time to time, as the law required they should be unmuzzled ( De 25:4 ), so that they grew fat in this work.
